name: Design Matrices
description:
A design matrix compares multiple concepts against a consistent set of criteria. Concepts are placed on one axis and criteria on another so that alternatives can be examined systematically.

The matrix helps make decision-making assumptions visible and can prevent teams from selecting concepts solely on intuition or enthusiasm. Its purpose is to structure judgement rather than produce an automatically correct answer.
whenToUse: Use a design matrix when several concepts have been generated and the team needs a transparent way to compare their relative strengths, limitations and trade-offs.
steps: Define criteria relevant to the project's goals and constraints.
Examine each concept against each criterion.
Record scores or qualitative judgements together with supporting reasoning.
Use the matrix to inform discussion rather than allowing totals alone to make the decision.
lookOutFor: Numbers can give subjective judgements an appearance of objectivity.
Criteria and weighting can predetermine which concepts appear successful.
Important qualities may be difficult to reduce to scores. Record reasoning alongside numerical ratings.

resources.citation: Pugh, S. (1991). *Total Design: Integrated Methods for Successful Product Engineering*. Addison-Wesley.
